newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech reforms must address capital mkts - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Czech reforms must address capital mkts - analysts.

text.p: A sweeping series of government measures to jump start the Czech economy, expected on Wednesday, must address capital market transparency or trading could dive into a major tailspin, analysts warned on Tuesday.
Tremours have rumbled through Czech markets over the past few days, as crown, debt and equity traders grow anxious about the contents of a pro-growth package due out mid-week.

The extent of budget cuts and measures affecting interest and exchange rates in the still-secret package -- aimed at stemming growing budget and trade deficits while reviving economic growth -- has kept everybody in the markets guessing.

Market analysts said that while the measures would focus on the trade deficit and wage growth, foreign investors would run for cover if problems in the capital markets, long seen as opaque and poorly regulated, were not addressed,.
"I think tomorrow's announcement will be more crucial to the capital markets than one might suspect," said Jeff Ocenasek, an equity trader at Atlantik Financni Trhy.

"We're looking forward to seeing what this will be, if it's something serious, something positive. If it is just window dressing, we're going to lose more capital than we have been, and foreign investors will stay away until the government looks like they're going to get serious," he added.
Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus and other senior ministers have suggested a series of budget cuts along with a loosening in monetary policy, but specific details have not been revealed.
In addition, officials have also indicated that Klaus will push for an independent market watchdog based on the U.S. Securities Exchange Commission (SEC).

The package, which Klaus said on Sunday would include both short- and long-term measures, is also expected to strengthen powers for officials investigating financial crimes, as well as moves to bring more market transparency in general.
The Prague Stock Exchange's PX50 index fell 5.1 points to 543.4 at the daily price fixing on Tuesday, putting the index down some 14 percent since mid-February.
Foreign investors, tired of a market that sees well over half of trading take place in virtual secrecy off-market, have been at the heart of a sell-off that triggered the fall.

"I think that if we have a timetable and something clear on the SEC, we'll see more capital inflows from international investors, especially into equities but also into the bond market," said one London-based analyst.

Jan Cerba, a bond trader at ING Barings, added: "People are expecting the bond market to react positively. We are missing foreign investors here, and if the measures both economic ones and market ones are strong, this could help bring them."
The Czech central bank (CNB) took the first step in the process last Thursday by easing minimum reserve requirements to 9.5 percent from 11.5 percent, but kept key interest rates unchanged.
The Czech crown fell to a 10-month low in early Tuesday trading, losing over one percent against its dollar/mark basket parity to around 2.30 percent on the devaluation side of the mid-point.
The crown, which hit its high in February against the central bank's mark/dollar peg, has been especially sensitive as government pressure for an easing of monetary policy grows.

CNB officials have since said that a rate cut is not in the cards, but analysts said possible changes to the band within which the central bank fixes the crown -- also rumoured to be part of the package -- have been pushing the crown lower.
Traders are also debating whether the central bank, as a complicit part of the plan to be announced on Wednesday, would let the crown depreciate to help a worsening trade situation.

The government and the central bank have repeatedly ruled out a direct administrative devaluation of the crown in order to boost exports, although the country's current account deficit now is over eight percent of gross domestic product.
